title: At the market

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Tawad nang kaunti
dialogs.intro: A wet market in Quiapo. Budi is with Mia, buying fruit and vegetables for the week.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Ate, how much are the mangoes?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ang mahal naman! Puwede po bang tumawad?
lines.id: That's expensive! May I bargain, ma'am?
lines.literal: how expensive indeed! possible ma'am [question] to-bargain?

lines.speaker: Tindera:
lines.text: Sige, setenta na lang. Sariwa iyan, galing Cebu.
lines.id: All right, seventy then. They're fresh, from Cebu.
lines.literal: all-right, seventy now just. fresh that, from Cebu.

lines.speaker: Mia:
lines.text: Kuya, dalawang kilo na lang para mura.
lines.id: Kuya, just take two kilos so it's cheaper.
lines.literal: older-brother, two kilo now just so cheap.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sige. Dalawang kilo po. Pabili rin po ng kamatis.
lines.id: Okay. Two kilos, ma'am. And I'd like to buy some tomatoes too.
lines.literal: all-right. two kilo ma'am. please-buy also ma'am of tomato.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Anim na piraso. At isang tali na sibuyas.
lines.id: Six pieces. And one bunch of onions.
lines.literal: six piece. and one bunch that onion.

lines.speaker: Tindera:
lines.text: Ayan po. Isang daan at bente lahat.
lines.id: Here you go, sir. A hundred and twenty in all.
lines.literal: there-it-is sir. one hundred and twenty all.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Heto po ang bayad. Salamat po, ate!
lines.id: Here's the payment. Thank you, ate!
lines.literal: here-it-is ma'am si payment. thanks ma'am, older-sister!

lines.speaker: Tindera:
lines.text: Salamat din! Balik po kayo, ha?
lines.id: Thank you too! Come back again, okay?
lines.literal: thanks also! return sir you-all, okay?

notes: **Ate and kuya are used with strangers.** Addressing a vendor as *ate* or *kuya* isn't small talk, it's basic manners. For someone much older: *nanay*, *tatay*, *lola*, *lolo*. Skipping them makes you sound cold.

**Pabili is the magic word at a stall.** Literally "please buy for me", it begins nearly every small transaction: *Pabili po ng tubig.* Family members: *pahingi* (ask for), *pakiabot* (please pass), *pakibigyan* (please give).

**Tumawad means to bargain.** Bargaining in a wet market is normal and expected; in malls and shops with price tags, it isn't. *Puwede po bang tumawad?* asks permission first and will never be taken as rude.
**Ang mahal naman!** uses *naman* to soften the complaint. Without *naman*, *ang mahal!* sounds like an accusation; with *naman*, it's a playful invitation to lower the price.
**Na lang marks a final offer**: *setenta na lang* = "seventy then, just". This is the characteristic sound of Philippine bargaining, and it almost always closes the deal.
**Piraso** (from Spanish *pieza*) means "piece", used for things counted one by one. *Tali* means a bunch or tied bundle.
**Isang daan at bente** shows a mixture of the two number systems in one price: the hundreds are native numbers, the tens are Spanish. This is very common and no one considers it wrong.
**Sariwa** means fresh. You'll hear this word often as the seller's reason for holding the price — and as praise when you really get good produce.
**Galing Cebu** shortens *galing sa Cebu*. In fast speech, *sa* often drops after *galing* when a place name follows.

grammars.title: Asking politely — the paki- family
body: Tagalog has one prefix whose only job is to make a request sound polite. It attaches in front of a verb and instantly turns a command into a plea.

head: Form
Literal
Used for
Example
rows: asking someone to hand it over

after: All these forms are polite on their own, but *po* is still added for older or unfamiliar people. Adding *po* is never wrong.
The thing requested takes *ng*: *pabili po **ng** tubig*, *pahingi po **ng** tissue*. The person addressed takes *sa* or *kay*: *pakibigay po **kay** Ben*.
The shortest form that's still polite at a stall: say the item, the amount, then *po*. *Dalawang tubig po.* That's enough, and it's what real people say.

grammars.title: Units and quantities
body: Most Philippine units come from Spanish, and others are market units with no exact equivalent in English.
after: The sachet unit deserves its own mention: in the Philippines nearly every household item is sold in single-use packets — shampoo, coffee, soy sauce, detergent. This *tingi-tingi* (retail by the piece) economy is the everyday face of the sari-sari store.

*Tingi* means buying in small retail amounts: *Tingi po, dalawang sachet lang.* There's no exact English word for it, though the practice will be familiar to anyone who has bought a single cigarette or a one-shot coffee packet.

blocks.text: *Sa uulitin* literally means "to the one to be repeated" and is used when leaving without buying, or when saying goodbye after being hosted. It's polite and not awkward — far better than slipping away silently.

blocks.title: Unwritten rules of bargaining
items: Bargain at wet markets and street stalls; don't bargain in shops with price tags, pharmacies or restaurants.
Bargaining with a smile and one joke almost always works; bargaining with a serious face rarely does.
If the vendor refuses and you buy anyway, say thank you as usual. Bargaining is not a fight, and mustn't be treated like one.

blocks.text: *Itim* and *puti* are two words you barely need to memorize if you know Malay or Indonesian: they're direct cousins of *hitam* and *putih*. Note also *kayumanggi*, a word with no exact English equivalent that carries its own pride in the Philippines.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right unit: kilo, piraso, dosena, tali, bote.
Turn into a polite request with paki- or pa-. Example: Bumili ka ng tubig. → Pabili po ng tubig.
Put the words in the right order.
